episodes.167304: There was an evening marine thunderstorm wind gust.
episodes.167309: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed around midday into the early afternoon along and ahead of a cold front.  Multiple reports of trees being snapped or uprooted were received in Madison and Jackson Counties.
episodes.167310: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed around midday into the early afternoon along and ahead of a cold front.  A couple of reports of trees being knocked down were received.
episodes.167434: Isolated late day thunderstorms across southern central Indiana included a slow-moving cell in northeastern Jackson County that spawned a weak and very brief landspout tornado.
episodes.167491: A line of severe thunderstorms organized to the west of the area during the early morning hours and raced across the area during the morning. The storms produced several reports of wind damage along with two tornadoes.
episodes.167619: A slow moving low pressure system, along with plenty of moisture, allowed for showers and thunderstorms to gradually move through the Ohio Valley during the day on May 6th. Heavy rainfall occurred with these storms and additional storm and shower activity developed over the same areas. A swath of 3 to 4 inches of rain fell in a narrow corridor from Huntington northeastward to Elkins, with a few isolated pockets of 4 to 5 reported. This led to considerable flash flooding. A few stronger storms also developed, one of which led to an area of tree damage in Randolph County.||Multiple water rescues took place throughout the Metro Valley, including a man who was swept away while working on his tractor in Cabell County. Additionally, several vehicles were submerged in flood waters and over one hundred homes were impacted by high water with the hardest hit area being the Enslow Park community of Huntington. Flooding occurred across many roadways throughout West Virginia, leaving multiple roads impassable for a time until the water receded.||Even after the rain had concluded, several rivers in the state rose out of their banks for the next several days. This resulted in flooding along areas adjacent to the rivers.
episodes.167631: Slow moving showers and thunderstorms produced locally heavy rainfall as a low pressure system moved east along a stationary boundary situated across the Ohio Valley.
episodes.167632: Slow moving showers and thunderstorms produced locally heavy rainfall as a low pressure system moved east along a stationary boundary situated across the Ohio Valley.
episodes.167686: A mid-upper level trough approached the area by afternoon with a broad area of divergence and strong flow thanks to an associated jet streak. A surface warm front, connected to a developing low pressure center over the Ohio Valley, lifted north of the area by early afternoon. An alley of 2000+ J/kg of CAPE was present by mid-afternoon and mid-level dry air preceded the surface cold front, both combining for an enhanced wind and hail threat. With strong deep layer shear over 50 knots, the surface front forced convection quickly became severe. Significant hail was reported in the Augusta area and widespread wind damage was reported across the entire CSRA.
episodes.168104: Numerous supercell thunderstorms tracked northeast across East Tennessee, starting in the late morning hours and continuing into the evening. Many of the storms produced damaging wind gusts and large hail, mainly in central and northern portions of the Tennessee Valley. Although several storms exhibited rotation signatures on radar, no tornadoes were confirmed.
episodes.168105: Numerous supercell thunderstorms tracked northeast across East Tennessee and into southwest Virginia in the late afternoon and evening. The storms produced damaging wind gusts and large hail in Washington County. Although some storms exhibited rotation signatures on radar, no tornadoes were reported.
episodes.168106: Numerous supercell thunderstorms tracked northeast across East Tennessee and the southern Appalachians. One storm tracked across extreme southwest North Carolina, and produced large hail.
episodes.168114: A warm front was in place across the state during the morning hours on May 6th, setting the stage for increased moisture and warm air into the region. By the afternoon, a nearby low pressure system began to occlude, furthering the lift and instability across the state. Showers and thunderstorms developed across much of the region throughout the day, becoming strong to severe by mid-day. Flooding and wind damage was reported throughout the afternoon and into the evening. A tornado was also reported and confirmed near General Burnside in Pulaski County during the early afternoon hours.
episodes.168152: A mid-upper level trough approached the area by afternoon with a broad area of divergence and strong flow thanks to an associated jet streak. A surface warm front, connected to a developing low pressure center over the Ohio Valley, lifted north of the area by early afternoon. An alley of 2000+ J/kg of CAPE was present by mid-afternoon and mid-level dry air preceded the surface cold front, both combining for an enhanced wind and hail threat. With strong deep layer shear over 50 knots, the surface front forced convection quickly became severe.
episodes.168787: Strong to severe thunderstorms formed along a prefrontal trough in the evening which was driven by a potent mid level shortwave trough that slowly rotated across the Deep South through the following day. At the surface, a cyclone deepened as it tracked into the Tennessee/Ohio valleys during the evening and it resulted in a strengthening|low level wind field including a strong LLJ (around 50 kts) that lifted across the interior portions of SE GA with the core of the jet skirting just northwest of SE GA. As the LLJ|strengthened, an ongoing quasi-linear complex of storms pushed into SE GA along a SW-NE oriented prefrontal trough. Instability (1500-2000 j/kg) and shear (150-200 m2/s2) supported of all modes of severe weather (damaging wind, hail, and isolated tornadoes) as activity propagated into SE GA and portions of NE FL into the evening.
episodes.168957: Several rounds of severe storms developed in advance and along a cold front.  One of these storms produced damaging winds in Greenbrier County.
episodes.168959: Several rounds of severe storms developed in advance of a cold front. Multicellular clusters and supercells were the primary storm modes during this event which contributed to damaging winds, large hail, and one tornado.  CAPE values were 1,000 to 2,500 j/kg with helicity values near 300 m2/s2.
episodes.168988: Several rounds of severe thunderstorms developed along and in advance of a cold front. Multicellular clusters and supercells were the primary storm modes during this event which produced damaging winds, large hail and a brief EF-0 tornado. CAPE values of 1,000 to 2,500 j/kg and helicity values near 300 m2/s2 contributed to the widespread and organized nature of the storms.
episodes.169016: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in advance of an approaching cold front in the early afternoon hours across southeast Georgia. These thunderstorms produced large hail and damaging wind as they moved to the east.
episodes.169017: Clusters of severe thunderstorms developed in advance of an approaching cold front in the early afternoon hours across southeast Georgia. These thunderstorms moved eastward into southeast South Carolina and produced large hail and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.169041: A cluster of thunderstorms generated a funnel cloud ahead of a cold front in Robeson County NC.
episodes.169042: A large cluster of thunderstorms swept through portions of northeast SC ahead of a cold front.
episodes.169164: A cold front and strong upper level low pressure system moved through the region on the 5th. As this combined with afternoon heating, an unstable airmass and plenty of wind shear, severe storms developed. These storms brought damaging winds, and hail to the region.
episodes.169198: During the first week of the month, two storm systems moved out of the southern Plains. Scattered showers and thunderstorms brought around an inch of rain on average, while a few locations received up to 2.5 inches. Rises on the Mississippi River were sufficient for some minor flooding in a few areas.
episodes.169202: A thunderstorm complex produced isolated minor street flooding, followed by minor flooding of the St. Francis River. The thunderstorms were triggered by an early morning mesoscale convective vortex that tracked northeast from northwest Arkansas. A thunderstorm line propagated eastward, producing a short-duration heavy rain event. Over a wider region, enhanced low-level winds ahead of the convective vortex helped support a broad area of rain. Rainfall of 1 to 2 inches over a fairly short period of time was common.
episodes.169360: A late season cold front brought a round of strong to severe storms across the area.  Two brief tornadoes occurred, one in Perry and the other in the St Marks Wildlife Refuge.
episodes.169363: A late season cold front brought a round of showers and thunderstorms to the area with a couple of reports of severe weather.
episodes.169367: A late season cold front brought a round of strong to severe storms across the area.
episodes.169373: A cold front brought a round of strong thunderstorms to the area with a few gusts measured in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.169399: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across the marine area and produced strong wind gusts.
episodes.169400: A line of severe thunderstorms organized to the west of the area during the early morning hours and raced across the area during the morning. The storms produced several reports of wind damage along with two tornadoes.
episodes.169416: During the morning hours of May 5th, a surface warm front moved northward through central Kentucky before becoming nearly stationary near the Ohio River. South of this boundary, the atmosphere destabilized during the afternoon hours, allowing for clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms. Rain persisted across the region overnight from the 5th into the morning of the 6th as the surface low moved slowly to the east. On the 6th, more strong clusters of thunderstorms formed as a surface cold front passed through southern and central Kentucky. As a result of repeated rounds of heavy rainfall, some flash flooding occurred in the Cynthiana area on May 6th.
episodes.169476: Slow-moving low pressure provided rounds of rain to southwest Pennsylvania on May 6th-7th. Widespread 48 hour rainfall totals of 1 to 3 inches were observed, with locally higher amounts. Low-level convergence and frontogenesis fueled the heavier rainfall rates.  Flooding was noted in a few locations as streams overflowed their banks, resulting in road closures and trapped vehicles.
episodes.169617: A stalled front from the storm a system on May 2-3 moved northward back into the Ozarks as a warm front as a strong upper level low over southern Colorado moved eastward into the southern Plains. This led to another several rounds of widespread heavy rainfall that occurred from the late morning of the 4th to the early morning of the 6th, when the surface low exited the area. Widespread accumulations of two to five inches occurred, with isolated accumulations over six inches over parts of Jasper and Dade Counties. Numerous reports of flash flooding indicated that not only were low water crossings flooding, but major highways as well. Evacuations were conducted at both Roaring River State Park in Barry County and at Bennett Spring State Park on the Dallas/Laclede County Border. Several people were stranded in cabins and RVs at Bennett Spring during the peak of the flood. There were 11 swift water rescues reported in southwest Missouri. Unfortunately, there was one fatality in Dade County when a 65-year old male drove into a flooded low water crossing and was swept downstream after exiting his vehicle and attempting to swim to shore.
episodes.169670: An upper level trough moved across the southern Plains pushing a cold front into South Central Texas. Thunderstorms developed along the front and some of these storms produced large hail.
episodes.169765: Strong southerly flow lifted a warm front through central North Carolina Friday afternoon, triggering multiple rounds of severe and tornadic storms producing a radar confirmed tornado near the Orange/Alamance County line and hail up to golf ball size over the southern Piedmont and Sandhills. Numerous wind reports were also noted across the Sandhills and the Northwest and Northeast Piedmont.
episodes.169932: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed ahead of a frontal system throughout the afternoon and evening across upstate South Carolina. Several of the storms produced brief large hail and damaging winds, while an EF1 tornado developed in Pickens County.
episodes.169944: A Pacific weather system and its associated cold front brought a round of strong winds to the Rocky Mountain Front, the Plains, and portions of Southwest Montana. Shower and thunderstorm development occurred along and ahead of the front and produced localized severe weather. A strong pressure gradient due to lee side troughing over the Canadian Prairies also contributed to strong non-convective wind gusts.
episodes.169968: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed ahead of a frontal system throughout the afternoon and evening across western North Carolina. Several of the storms produced brief large hail and damaging winds, while an EF1 tornado developed in Swain  County.
episodes.169979: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and early evening. Some of the storms became severe and produced damaging winds, along with some large hail.
episodes.170034: A cold front was moving through the local area from the northwest in the early morning hours of May 6th. A line of showers and thunderstorms had formed along the frontal boundary. Although the post frontal airmass was stable, 70 degree dewpoints just ahead of the front provided just enough buoyancy and instability for a couple severe thunderstorms to develop and produce damaging winds.
episodes.170051: A strong cold front pushed through the area during prime heating hours during the afternoon of May 6th. This frontal passage in combination with high levels of instability along the front produced widespread wind damage reports across portions of central Georgia.
episodes.170114: A cold front was moving through the local area from the northwest in the early morning hours of May 6th. A line of showers and thunderstorms had formed along the frontal boundary. Although the post frontal airmass was stable, 70 degree dewpoints just ahead of the front provided just enough buoyancy and instability for a couple severe thunderstorms to develop and produce damaging winds.
episodes.170127: Heavy rains brought river flooding to portions of the Ouachita, Black, Spring, White, and Cache Rivers.
episodes.170156: A potent upper level shortwave trough coupled with a cold front passage at the surface provided showery activity through most of the day. During the afternoon, these systems interacted with increasing instability, strong bulk shear, and upsloping into mountain areas allowed some of these showers to strengthen into strong thunderstorms that produced severe hail and a tornado.
episodes.170272: Showers developing over the offshore waters during the early morning hours spawned a waterspout off Miami Beach.
episodes.170296: A line of thunderstorms crossing a warm front caused several instances of flooding across MD on May 6th into May 7th. Residual river flooding continued through May 9th due to excessive runoff.
episodes.170313: An area of low pressure tracked from the Mississippi Valley into the Ohio valley on May 6 with the associated warm front lifting north from South Carolina towards the Virginia/North Carolina border. The main low occluded during the day with a secondary low forming in western North Carolina during the evening. Scattered storms developed across central North Carolina during the afternoon, moving northeast into southeast Virginia while interacting with the warm front. A second round of storms developed in association with the secondary surface low late in the afternoon and into the evening in western North Carolina, tracking into southern and central Virginia during the evening.
episodes.170314: An area of low pressure tracked from the Mississippi Valley into the Ohio valley on May 6 with the associated warm front lifting north from South Carolina towards the Virginia/North Carolina border. The main low occluded during the day with a secondary low forming in western North Carolina during the evening. Scattered storms developed across central North Carolina during the afternoon, moving northeast into southeast Virginia while interacting with the warm front. A second round of storms developed in association with the secondary surface low late in the afternoon and into the evening in western North Carolina, tracking into southern and central Virginia during the evening.
episodes.170451: Heavy rain brought flooding to parts of Arkansas during early to mid May, 2022. Very heavy rain fell from northeast Oklahoma eastward into Arkansas and across southern Missouri. This widespread heavy rain led to rises on area rivers as well as some flash flooding.
episodes.170493: Scattered multicell and a few supercell thunderstorms affected parts of Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening hours on May 5. One supercell caused significant hail and wind damage across Cannon and White Counties.
episodes.170494: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed across Middle Tennessee during the during on May 6. Several reports of large hail and wind damage were received.

A tornado touched down two miles east of Mebane at 5:08 PM EDT. Damage at this location consisted of a brick wall of a large manufacturing facility that was blown over. The tornado then continued to move approximately 3.6 miles to the northeast before lifting and dissipating at 5:15 PM EDT.  Along the track, damage consisted of mostly uprooted hardwood trees and snapped softwood or pine trees. In several cases, the trees fell onto homes, which resulted in damage to the homes. At least one detached garage was completely destroyed and its roof and walls were scattered in nearly all directions. At this location, the damage path width was at its widest, measuring nearly 400 yards wide. Tree damage became more widely scattered and less intense approximately 4 miles northeast of Mebane, where the tornado subsequently lifted.

A tornado touched down briefly in downtown Perry, FL and was on the ground for about a minute. The tornado touched down west of South Quincy St. near W. Homer J. Smith Ave. It blew over a fence and pealed back a tin roof at a tavern. It continued east northeast along E. Hampton Springs Rd pulling up a carport cover that was anchored to the ground. The tornado bent over a stop sign and snapped large branches off a tree near the intersection of S. Jefferson St. and W. Hampton Springs Rd. One of these was hurled across the intersection, breaking a window of a home. The tornado then broke or bent several large tree limbs before damaging a fence east of Orange St. The tornado lifted just east of S. Center St.  This tornado was rated EF0 with max winds around 75 mph.
